title: Unsafer in Many Turns: Benchmarking and Defending Multi-Turn Safety Risks in Tool-Using Agents
claim: Capability outpaces safety; we introduce a taxonomy-built multi-turn benchmark that exposes degraded safety, plus a self-exploration defense that restores it.
layout: 3 panels: top benchmark flow left-to-right, bottom-left gap plot, bottom-right defense pipeline
description: The figure has three rounded panels. The top blue panel, titled MultiTurn-AgentRisk Benchmark, flows left to right. A tool icon strip (folder, Notion, terminal, Chrome) leads to a single-turn harmful command, 'Run rm -rf /', which is refused (green shield). An arrow leads to an Attack Taxonomy box with two branches, Addition and Decomposition, each shown with small square diagrams. A further arrow leads to a three-turn attack sequence in green and red shading, labeled 'ASR +16%' with a warning icon. The bottom-left gray panel, Capability-Safety Gap, plots a rising blue capability curve against a flat red safety curve with a dashed gap line. The bottom-right green panel, ToolShield: Capability → Safety, shows a New tool feeding a Self-exploration pipeline of Generate test cases, Simulate execution and Distill experience. It outputs a safe turn sequence labeled 'ASR −30%' with a check shield.
caption: As agents' capabilities grow, their safety falls behind, opening a widening capability-safety gap. To scale agent safety evaluation, we develop an attack taxonomy that transforms single-turn harmful tasks to multi-turn attack sequences. Applying the taxonomy, we construct \ours, the first agent safety benchmark in multi-turn, tool-realistic settings. To mitigate these risks, we propose \oursdef, a self-exploration defense that effectively protects tool-using agents in multi-turn interactions.
abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable, yet their safety lags behind. This creates a gap between what agents can do and should do. This gap widens as agents engage in multi-turn interactions and employ diverse tools, introducing new risks overlooked by existing benchmarks. To systematically scale safety testing into multi-turn, tool-realistic settings, we propose a principled taxonomy that transforms single-turn harmful tasks into multi-turn attack sequences. Using this taxonomy, we construct MT-AgentRisk (Multi-Turn Agent Risk Benchmark), the first benchmark to evaluate multi-turn tool-using agent safety. Our experiments reveal substantial safety degradation: the Attack Success Rate (ASR) increases by 16% on average across open and closed models in multi-turn settings. To close this gap, we propose ToolShield, a training-free, tool-agnostic, self-exploration defense: when encountering a new tool, the agent autonomously generates test cases, executes them to observe downstream effects, and distills safety experiences for deployment. Experiments show that ToolShield effectively reduces ASR by 30% on average in multi-turn interactions. Our code is available at https://github.com/CHATS-lab/ToolShield.
